risk_rationale: Inflation remains materially above the Fed's 2% target on both CPI (3.7% as of September 2026) and PCE (3.6%) measures, keeping real rates restrictive and policy options constrained. The 10Y at 5.07% with a 7.28% mortgage rate is actively compressing consumer balance sheets, while a saving rate of 3.8% and rising CC delinquencies signal waning household buffer capacity. A positive but narrowing term premium and sticky services inflation leave little room for a policy pivot without reigniting price pressures.
outlook_headline: Resilient growth masks mounting consumer stress as inflation stays too hot, long rates bite hard, and the Fed has no clean exit.
outlook_body: Real GDP growth of 3.4% annualized is running above trend, but this strength is increasingly inconsistent with the Fed's inflation mandate and risks extending the restrictive rate environment further into 2027. Headline CPI eased to 3.7% in September 2026 — a 36bp drop from the prior reading — but Core PCE at 3.1% confirms underlying price pressure is not resolved. Consumer fundamentals are deteriorating at the margin: a 3.8% saving rate, 2.9% credit card delinquency, and a 7.28% mortgage rate collectively tighten the vice on discretionary spending. Allocators should maintain defensive positioning; the asymmetry of risks favors duration caution and credit selectivity over spread compression plays.

tabs.gdp: Q3 2026 real GDP printed 3.4% annualized, well above consensus and driven by resilient consumer spending and inventory build — both components that warrant scrutiny for durability. Elevated long-end rates (10Y at 5.07%) are a recognized late-cycle drag on capex and residential investment, suggesting momentum likely fades in coming quarters. The risk is a sharper-than-expected deceleration as fiscal impulse normalizes and credit tightening feeds through with the typical 4-6 quarter lag.
tabs.jobs: November's NFP at 165K is a solid but moderating print, consistent with a labor market decelerating from its 2024-2025 pace rather than deteriorating outright. Leading indicators — temp employment, hours worked, and job openings — bear close monitoring as lagging confirmation of strength can mask turning points. At this pace, monthly job creation is roughly in line with labor force growth, leaving little slack buffer if demand softens abruptly.
tabs.unemp: U-3 unemployment holds at 4.1%, which remains near historical norms but has drifted up from the cycle low, consistent with a late-cycle softening. The U-6 underemployment rate at 7.9% represents a material spread of 3.8 percentage points over U-3, flagging that involuntary part-time and marginally attached workers are accumulating — a leading indicator of broader labor market deterioration. This divergence between headline and broad unemployment warrants elevated attention; it typically widens ahead of U-3 inflections.
tabs.wages: Wage growth of 3.9% YoY is running above what is compatible with 2% inflation on a sustained basis, assuming trend productivity growth in the 1.5-2.0% range. Real wage growth is marginally positive versus September CPI of 3.7%, offering only thin purchasing power gains that do not fully offset the wealth erosion from higher borrowing costs and reduced asset prices. The persistence of 3.9% wage growth will keep the Fed alert to second-round inflation effects, particularly in services-heavy CPI components.
tabs.cpi: September 2026 headline CPI YoY fell to 3.7%, a notable 36bp deceleration from the prior reading and the most significant improvement flagged in the current snapshot — no October 2026 CPI YoY figure is available due to a BLS data gap. Core CPI at 2.6% is approaching target but has stalled in the mid-2% range for multiple months, indicating the last mile of disinflation remains the hardest. The Fed cannot declare victory: a 110bp gap between headline CPI and the 2% target, combined with Core PCE at 3.1%, ensures policy remains restrictive through at least Q2 2027.
tabs.pce: PCE YoY at 3.6% and Core PCE at 3.1% confirm that the Fed's preferred inflation gauge remains decisively above target, with core running 110bp over the 2% mandate. The personal saving rate of 3.8% is low by historical standards and leaves consumers with limited capacity to absorb additional price increases or income shocks. Together, these readings indicate consumer spending resilience is increasingly debt- and income-flow-dependent rather than balance-sheet-driven — a fragile foundation for sustained growth.
tabs.yield: The 10Y-2Y spread has re-steepened to +27bp after an extended inversion, but the absolute level of rates — 10Y at 5.07% and 2Y at 4.80% — remains acutely restrictive across the curve. The Fed Funds rate at 3.88% sits below the 2Y yield, a configuration that signals markets are pricing continued policy restraint rather than imminent easing. Any move toward cuts is conditional on sustained Core PCE deceleration below 2.5%; absent that, the front end remains anchored and long-end volatility risk is elevated.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 93bp and HY OAS at 347bp reflect credit markets pricing a soft-landing scenario with contained default risk — spreads are tighter than historical recession medians and arguably complacent given the macro backdrop. With the 10Y at 5.07%, all-in IG yields are well above 6%, which is mechanically competing with equity earnings yields for institutional allocation. HY at 347bp over Treasuries fails to adequately compensate for late-cycle credit deterioration risk; expect spread widening if labor market softening accelerates or refinancing stress emerges.
tabs.housing: A 30Y mortgage rate of 7.28% remains severely restrictive for housing affordability, locking existing homeowners into sub-4% legacy mortgages and suppressing transaction volume — a lock-in effect with no near-term resolution absent material rate relief. Housing starts of 1,309K annualized show the new construction market is partially filling the existing home supply gap, but builder activity is constrained by financing costs on both the production and purchase side. Residential investment will remain a net drag on GDP growth until mortgage rates decline meaningfully, which requires either a Fed pivot or a significant Treasury yield rally.
tabs.oil: WTI at $89.5 and Brent at $92.9 represent an elevated energy price environment that feeds directly into headline inflation and acts as a regressive tax on consumer spending capacity. At these levels, gasoline and energy services components will continue to exert upward pressure on CPI headline, complicating the Fed's disinflation narrative. Supply-side tightness — whether OPEC+ production discipline or geopolitical risk premium — means oil represents a bilateral inflation risk; a move toward $95+ Brent would likely delay any Fed easing timeline materially.
tabs.banks: Credit card delinquency at 2.9% is rising and signals that consumer credit stress is building — banks with high revolving credit exposure face deteriorating asset quality into 2027. Net interest income (NII) is structurally supported by the high-rate environment, but deposit repricing pressure is intensifying as savers migrate to money market funds, compressing net interest margins at the margin. Banks face a deteriorating credit quality / rate-peak combination: the best NII tailwinds are likely behind them while provision expenses are building, making sector earnings upgrades increasingly difficult to justify.

signal_flags.note: Largest single-period deceleration in the current snapshot; directionally encouraging but headline remains 170bp above target. No October 2026 YoY CPI is available due to BLS data gap — trend confirmation is suspended until November data is published.

At 5.07%, the 10Y is at cycle highs and transmitting severe tightening into mortgages, corporate financing, and equity valuations. Sustained at this level, duration risk in fixed income portfolios and refinancing risk for leveraged borrowers is acute.
Running 110bp above the Fed's 2% target on the preferred policy inflation gauge; forecloses any near-term pivot and reinforces an extended on-hold stance that keeps financial conditions restrictive.

Historically extreme level crushing housing affordability and transaction volumes; reinforces lock-in effect suppressing existing home supply and generating a structural drag on residential investment and consumer mobility.

Wide U-6/U-3 spread indicates slack is accumulating in part-time and marginally attached categories; historically this divergence precedes U-3 deterioration by 2-3 quarters and should be monitored as a leading labor market stress indicator.
Rising delinquency rate points to consumer credit stress building beneath resilient aggregate spending data; a deteriorating leading indicator for bank provisioning and consumer discretionary demand.

Below the long-run average and providing thin cushion against income or employment shocks; consumer spending resilience is increasingly reliant on credit rather than accumulated savings, raising the risk of a sharper spending retrenchment.
Elevated oil prices sustain headline CPI pressure and risk derailing the disinflation trajectory; a move above $95 would materially complicate the Fed's path to easing.
